questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Write short historical notes on the **activities** of any **TWO** of the following structures of the League of Nations: the ILO, the Mandate Commission, the Disarmament Commission, the Refugee Commission, the Health Commission, the Assembly.

[10 marks: 5 for each of the two structures chosen, activities and importance together being marked 5/5/5/5 in the printed paper]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The League of Nations (created in 1919-1920, with its headquarters at Geneva) had several organs and special bodies for its work. A candidate chooses **any two** of the following.

**a) The ILO (International Labour Organisation).** Created in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles, it was a **tripartite body** in which representatives of governments, employers and workers met in an annual conference. Its first Director was Albert Thomas (France). Its activities were: collecting and publishing information on working conditions; adopting international **conventions and recommendations** on hours of work (the eight-hour day), minimum age for work, the protection of women and children, accident compensation and conditions of seamen; and urging member states to adopt them as national laws.

**b) The Mandate Commission (Permanent Mandates Commission).** It was made up of experts, mostly from colonial powers, who **supervised the former German and Ottoman territories** given as mandates (A, B and C mandates) to Britain, France, Belgium, Japan, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand, including Cameroon and Togo. Its activities were: examining the **annual reports** of the mandatory powers, hearing their representatives, receiving petitions from the inhabitants, and making recommendations to the Council.

**c) The Disarmament Commission.** It worked on the Covenant's promise to reduce armaments "to the lowest point consistent with national safety". Its activities included the Temporary Mixed Commission (1920-1924) and the Preparatory Commission, which studied ways of limiting arms; it drafted the **Geneva Protocol (1924)** on arbitration and security (not adopted); and it prepared the **World Disarmament Conference (1932-1934)** at Geneva.

**d) The Refugee Commission.** The League's High Commissioner for Refugees, **Fridtjof Nansen** of Norway (appointed in 1921), organised the **return of prisoners of war** from Russia to their homes (hundreds of thousands), and helped Russian, Armenian and Greek-Turkish refugees. His activities included the **"Nansen passport"**, an identity document for stateless refugees (1922), and the resettlement and housing of refugees in other countries, and of people exchanged between Greece and Turkey (1923).

**e) The Health Commission (Health Organisation).** It studied and fought **epidemics**: it helped to stop typhus in Eastern Europe, organised the fight against malaria, leprosy and tuberculosis, gathered **information on epidemics** and public health from all the world, and promoted common standards for medicines and vaccines.

**f) The Assembly.** The "parliament" of the League where all members were represented, each with **one vote**, and which met once a year in September at Geneva. Its activities included **admitting new members**, electing the non-permanent members of the Council, approving the **budget**, discussing disputes and international problems, and adopting recommendations, but decisions had to be unanimous.
themes: league of nations organs and agencies

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Write short historical notes on the **importance** of any **TWO** of the following structures of the League of Nations: the ILO, the Mandate Commission, the Disarmament Commission, the Refugee Commission, the Health Commission, the Assembly.

[10 marks: 5 for each of the two structures chosen, activities and importance together being marked 5/5/5/5 in the printed paper]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Although the League failed to keep the peace in the 1930s, several of its organs achieved real success. A candidate chooses **any two** of the following.

**a) The ILO.** It was one of the most **successful** parts of the League. It improved working conditions in many countries by setting international standards, and it showed that countries could cooperate for social progress. The ILO survived the League of Nations and, in 1946, became a **specialised agency of the United Nations**, which it remains to this day.

**b) The Mandate Commission.** It was important because it made the colonial powers **responsible to an international body** for the territories they governed and so introduced the idea that colonies were a "sacred trust of civilisation". But its power was limited: it had no means to force the mandatory powers to follow its advice, so the mandates were in practice often treated like colonies. The system was a model for the **UN trusteeship system** after 1945 (which concerned Cameroon, Togo and others).

**c) The Disarmament Commission.** It showed the **failure of the League**. The Great Powers did not wish to reduce their arms. The World Disarmament Conference (1932-1934) failed, and when Hitler withdrew Germany from the Conference and the League in October 1933, the effort to limit arms collapsed. This failure contributed to the arms race of the 1930s and the weakening of collective security.

**d) The Refugee Commission.** It was important because it saved the lives of hundreds of thousands of people, gave refugees legal status through the Nansen passport and began an **international way of caring for refugees**, which was later continued by the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR, 1950). Nansen was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922.

**e) The Health Commission.** It was a **success** as it fought epidemics, collected world health statistics and encouraged international cooperation in medicine. It was the forerunner of the **World Health Organisation** (WHO, 1948).

**f) The Assembly.** It was important as the first world forum where **all states, large and small, could meet** and speak on equal terms; it permitted open discussion of international problems and helped to create world public opinion. It was weak because of the rule of unanimity and the absence of the USA and, for periods, of Germany and the Soviet Union, and it could not take decisive action against aggressors in the 1930s (Manchuria, Abyssinia). It was the model for the **General Assembly of the UN**.
themes: league of nations organs and agencies
